div.p: In their widely-cited survey on mixed-criticality systems, Burns and Davis describe a very general model for representing mixed-criticality sporadic tasks. In this general model multiple estimates, at differing levels of assurance, are specified for each of the three parameters -worst-case execution time (WCET), relative deadline, and period -characterizing a 3-parameter sporadic task. The preemptive uniprocessor scheduling of systems of such tasks is considered. A scheduling algorithm is presented, proved correct, and quantitatively characterized via the speedup factor metric for dual-criticality systems of such tasks. To our knowledge, this is the first work to conduct any form of analysis of task systems that are represented using this general model.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the 3-parameter sporadic task model that is widely used in real-time scheduling theory, each task is characterized by three parameters: a worst-case execution time (WCET), a period, and a relative deadline. Mixed-criticality scheduling theory seeks to obtain resource-efficient implementations of systems in which functionalities of two or more distinct criticalities are implemented upon a shared platform. It primarily seeks to obtain such efficient implementations by developing techniques to exploit an insight of Vestal [16] that the exact values of the parameters characterizing tasks are often not known beforehand; instead these values must be estimated. The level of assurance at which parameters should be estimated in order to ensure correctness of more critical functionalities is typically greater than the level of assurance at which they must be estimated in order to ensure correctness of less critical functionalities.

Much prior research on the mixed-criticality scheduling of systems of 3-parameter sporadic tasks (see, e.g., the survey [12] by Burns & Davis) has focused upon models in which multiple values have been provided for the WCET parameter of each task, the different values representing estimates, at different levels of assurance, of the actual WCET of the task. A few papers (e.g., [1], [8], [11]) have considered models in which multiple estimates are provided for the period parameter characterizing each task. The motivation for this is that sporadic tasks typically represent event-triggered phenomena, with the task's period parameter denoting the minimum duration of time between the occurrence of successive triggering events. In many cases, this minimum inter-triggering duration is not known precisely but must be estimated; it may therefore make sense, in a mixed-criticality setting, to specify multiple estimates for this parameter with smaller values representing safer (more conservative) estimates that one may trust to higher levels of assurance than larger values.

We thus see that prior work has considered mixed-criticality models in which multiple estimates are provided for the WCET and the period parameters. In their survey [12], Burns and Davis briefly mention a further possible generalization, in which multiple estimates are provided for each of the three parameters: WCET, period, and relative deadline. In this more general model, it is assumed (as in the prior models) that WCET estimates are non-decreasing with increasing criticality (i.e., more conservative WCET estimates tend to be larger than less conservative ones), and that period estimates are nonincreasing with increasing criticality (i.e., more conservative period estimates tend to be smaller than less conservative ones). The assumption they make regarding relative deadline estimates is, however, novel to the best of our knowledge: they assume that relative deadline estimates are non-decreasing with increasing criticality (i.e., more conservative relative deadline estimates tend to be larger than less conservative ones). This might run counter to one's first instincts, and merits some discussion: the rationale is that the larger deadlines correspond to the safety-critical correctness requirementsthese are the "true" deadlines that must be met in order to ensure correct functioning of the safety-critical functionalities. The smaller deadlines correspond to lower-criticality quality of service (QoS) constraints, in that meeting them allows for the optimization of QoS in a manner that does not directly impact upon the correctness of the safety-critical functionalities. One could, for instance, envision a system in which some value that is needed for some critical functionality must be computed by a particular deadline, but computing it by an earlier deadline would additionally allow for this value to be used as input to some non-critical QoS functionality. Related work. We will not review here the rich body of research that exists concerning the mixed-criticality scheduling of task systems with multiple WCET estimates -see [12] for a comprehensive survey. With regards to systems in which multiple estimates are provided for the period parameters, the preemptive uniprocessor EDF-based scheduling of such task systems was studied in [1], [2]; fixed-priority scheduling was studied in [8]. Burns and Davis [11] considered the scheduling of streams of periodic real-time traffic on controller-area networks (CANs), with the traffic streams being characterized by multiple period parameters at different levels of pessimism.

To our knowledge, the idea of providing multiple estimates of the relative deadline parameter was first proposed in [7]; however, the assumption in [7] about the estimates was the opposite of the one in [12] that we will be exploring in this paper. That is, it was suggested in [7] that the relative deadline parameter estimates should decrease with increasing criticality level; the stated rationale being that "the higher the criticality level, the greater the need for the task to complete well before any safety-critical timing constraint and hence the smaller the value of " the relative deadline parameter [7, page 150]. To our knowledge, this model of mixed-criticality systems has not been explored since being mentioned in [7]; we do not plan to study it any further in this paper.

This research. In this paper, we study the scheduling of mixed-criticality task systems specified according to the 3parameter sporadic tasks model in which multiple estimates are provided for all three parameters in the model of [12], upon preemptive uniprocessor platforms. As is fairly routine in the literature on mixed-criticality scheduling, we will primarily restrict our attention to dual-criticality systems -systems in which there are just two criticality levels specified, which we designate as LO and HI (with HI denoting the greater criticality). We seek to develop an algorithm for scheduling such systems, for which we are able to derive quantitative bounds upon its effectiveness. In order to do so, we propose a generalization to the EDF-VD scheduling algorithm [4] that schedules mixed-criticality sporadic task systems in which multiple values are only specified for the WCET parameter. Our generalization, which we call Algorithm EDFVD + , is able to deal with the more general mixed-criticality model of [12] that is considered in this paper, in which multiple values are specified for all three parameters -WCET, relative deadline, and period. It had previously been shown [5,Theorem 4.10] that EDF-VD has a speedup bound 1 no worse than (1 + √ 3/2), or ≈ 1.866, in scheduling dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task systems in which two values are specified only for WCETs. In [2], the same bound was shown to also hold for systems in which two values are specified only for the period parameters of tasks. In this paper, we prove that Algorithm EDFVD + has the same speedup bound when scheduling dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task systems with two values specified for WCETs, relative deadlines, and periods. From the perspective of the speedup bound metric, thus, Algorithm EDFVD + represents a strict improvement upon the current state of the art.

Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we detail and formally describe the task model we will be using in the remainder of this document, and provide a brief overview of some prior results that we will use. In Section III we present Algorithm EDFVD + , our algorithm for the scheduling of dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task systems in which two estimates are provided for the value of 1 Speedup bounds are one widely used metric for evaluating the effectiveness of scheduling algorithms, particularly on-line ones. We will define this metric in Section V. each parameter characterizing a task. We provide a formal proof of the correctness of this algorithm in Section IV; and derive some properties that characterize its effectiveness in Section V.

div.head: II. TASK MODEL & SOME PRIOR RESULTS
div.p: In the generalized 3-parameter mixed-criticality sporadic task model proposed in [12] , a sporadic task τ i is characterized by a 4-tuple (χ i , C i , D i , T i ), with χ i denoting the criticality of task τ i and each of the equi-sized vectors C i , D i , and T i denoting multiple estimates of the WCET, relative deadline, and period parameters of τ i . Assuming that the vectors represent estimates at increasing criticality levels, it is expected that • the components of C i are non-decreasing, indicating that more conservative WCET estimates tend to be larger than less conservative ones; • the components of D i are also non-decreasing, indicating that more conservative relative deadline estimates tend to be larger than less conservative ones; and • the components of T i are non-increasing, indicating that more conservative period estimates tend to be smaller than less conservative ones.

In this paper, we will, for the most part, restrict our attention to dual criticality systems -systems in which there are only two criticality levels defined. We denote these criticality levels as LO and HI, with LO-criticality tasks being less critical than HI-criticality ones. We will sometimes represent such dualcriticality tasks by enumerating all their parameters, in the following order:

div.p: A dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task system is a finite collection of independent such dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic tasks. We study the problem of scheduling such a task system, denoted τ , upon a fully preemptive uniprocessor.

Behaviors. Any execution of the system satisfying the properties that for each task τ i , each job of τ i completes upon receiving for at most C i (LO) units of execution and successive jobs of τ i arrive at least T i (LO) time units apart, is said to exhibit a LO-criticality behavior. Any execution of the An example dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task system.

system that does not exhibit LO-criticality behavior but which satisfies the property that for each task τ i , each job of τ i completes upon receiving at most C i (HI) units of execution and successive jobs of τ i arrive at least T i (HI) time units apart is said to exhibit a HI-criticality behavior. Any execution that does not exhibit HI-criticality or LO-criticality behavior is said to be erroneous.
Correctness. An algorithm for scheduling dual-criticality 3parameter sporadic task systems is said to be correct if and only if it satisfies the property that

• Each job of each task τ i completes execution within D i (LO) units of its arrival, in all LO-criticality behaviors of the system; and • Each job of each HI-criticality task τ i completes execution within D i (HI) units of arrival, in all HI-criticality behaviors of the system. An example. An example dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task system is depicted in Table I. As can be seen from the table, this system comprises two tasks, one each of LO and HI criticality. (This example has been constructed to focus attention on the multiple specifications of the relative deadline parameter; hence all the periods are assigned large enough values to ensure that successive jobs of the same task do not interfere with each other.) For this task system, consider a situation where jobs are generated by both tasks at the same instant in time.

• If the job of τ 2 is executed first and completes within 4 time units, we are in a LO-criticality behavior. However, τ 1 's job will not complete by the deadline of 5; hence, this is not a correct scheduling strategy. • Suppose instead that τ 1 's job were executed first, and τ 2 's job chosen for execution once τ 1 's job completes. If τ 2 's job does not complete upon being allocated 4 units of execution, we conclude that the system is exhibiting HI-criticality behavior. In the absence of the freedom to specify a HI-criticality relative deadline larger than the LO-criticality relative deadline, this strategy, too, would be incorrect since τ 2 's job would miss its deadline at 12. However, the added expressiveness of being able to specify the D 2 (HI) estimate of 20 means that this is in fact a correct scheduling strategy -τ 2 's job will indeed complete by this more relaxed deadline of 20 This example illustrates the benefits of the more general model of [12]; we are able to specify systems with a wider range of acceptable behaviors (i.e., behaviors that are deemed to be "correct"). Some prior results. The EDF-schedulability-analysis of systems of regular (not mixed-criticality) 3-parameter sporadic tasks on preemptive uniprocessors has been extensively studied (see, e.g. [14], [9], [3]); below, we briefly summarize some results that we will be using later in this document. For the remainder of this section, let τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) denote a regular 3-parameter sporadic task with WCET C i , relative deadline D i , and period T i .

Uniprocessor EDF-schedulability analysis algorithms for 3parameter sporadic task systems make use of the concept of the demand bound function [9]; the demand bound function DBF(τ i , t) of 3-parameter sporadic task τ i for an interval length t is defined as follows:
div.formula: DBF(τ i , t) def = max 0, t -D i T i + 1 × C i
div.p: The load of a 3-parameter sporadic task system τ is defined as follows:
div.formula: LOAD(τ ) def = max t≥0 τi∈τ DBF(τ i , t) t

div.p: is a necessary and sufficient condition for the EDFschedulability of 3-parameter sporadic task systems τ upon a unit-speed preemptive uniprocessor. Although computing LOAD(τ ) may in general take time exponential in the representation of τ , pseudo-polynomial algorithms are known [9], [15], [17] for doing so for task systems τ possessing the additional property that the utilization of τ -the quantity ( τi∈τ C i /T i ) -is bounded from above by a constant strictly smaller than 1. Polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS's) have also been derived that are able to compute an approximation to LOAD(τ ) in polynomial time, to any desired degree of accuracy [13].

div.head: III. ALGORITHM EDFVD +
div.p: We now derive an algorithm for scheduling dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task systems correctly upon a preemptive uniprocessor platform. Our algorithm is a generalization, to the more general dual-criticality task model considered in this paper, of the EDF-VD algorithm [4] that had previously been proposed for scheduling dual-criticality task systems in which WCET was the only parameter for which multiple estimated values were provided. In this paper, we are (as detailed in Section II) assuming dual estimates of relative deadlines and periods in addition to WCETs. Let τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } denote the task system that is to be scheduled, specified in this more general model. The essential idea behind EDF-VD (and hence, our algorithm as well) is to ensure that as long as system behavior is compliant with LO-criticality specifications, all HIcriticality jobs complete execution well before their deadlines -this guarantees that if the behavior ceases to be compliant with the LO-criticality specifications, there is sufficient computing capacity available to nevertheless complete all HI- criticality jobs by their deadlines (after discarding all LO- criticality jobs). More specifically, suppose that at some time instant t * either (a) a job of some task τ j does not complete despite having received C j (LO) units of execution; or (b) a job of some task τ j arrives less than T j (LO) time units after the arrival of the previous job of τ j .

The behavior is no longer compliant with LO-criticality specifications -we can say that a criticality level change has been triggered at time instant t * -and we are therefore not required to demonstrate correct execution of LO-criticality tasks and can discard all LO-criticality jobs. Informally, we would like to ensure for each HI-criticality task τ i (see Figure 2) that is active -arrived but not completed execution-at time t * that there is enough capacity available on the processor to ensure that τ i 's currently-active job completes execution by its deadline, provided only HI-criticality jobs execute henceforth.

To achieve this, we will ensure that as long as the system is behaving according to its LO-criticality specifications, τ i 's job would have completed well before its actual HI-criticality deadline (by d in Figure 2, where the actual HI-criticality deadline is denoted d). We will thus ensure that if it is active at time instant t * there is sufficient computing capacity freed up by the discarded LO-criticality tasks over the interval [d , d), to schedule τ i 's job to completion by its actual HI-criticality deadline, d.

In somewhat greater detail, we can think of our scheduling algorithm as consisting of three phases. The first phase is a pre-processing one: a schedulability test is applied to the system and if successful, a scaling parameter x is computed. This readies the system for the second, run-time phase of the algorithm. During this second phase, jobs are initially dispatched under the assumption that the system will behave according to the LO-criticality specifications. If this is violated -some job does not complete upon receiving up to its LO- criticality WCET, or successive jobs of some task arrive less than the task's LO-criticality period parameter time units apart -then the algorithm enters the third phase. During this third phase, only entered if the LO-criticality specifications are violated, the rules used for dispatching jobs change -among other things, all LO-criticality jobs are discarded and no further LO-criticality jobs will be admitted.

As can be seen from the pseudo-code in Figure 3, Algorithm EDFVD + either returns success (and computes a value for the scaling factor x), or it returns failure. This pre-processing phase is deemed successful if and only if Algorithm EDFVD + returns success, in which case the computed value of x is used as the scaling factor for HI-criticality deadlines by the run-time dispatcher described in Section III-B below in the subsequent, run-time phase. In Section IV we will show that if Algorithm EDFVD + returns success for a given task system τ , then τ is scheduled correctly by this run-time dispatcher.

div.head: B. Run-time dispatching
div.p: Dispatching of jobs during run-time occurs according to the following rules (these are essentially unchanged from the rules specified in [4]):

1) There is a criticality level indicator Γ, initialized to LO. 2) While (Γ ≡ LO), (this corresponds to the second phase of our algorithm as described in the overview.) a) If a job of task τ i ∈ τ arrives at time t, it is assigned a scheduling deadline as follows
div.formula: t + D i (LO) if χ i = LO t + min D i (LO), x × D i (HI) if χ i = HI.
div.p: That is, each LO-criticality job is assigned a deadline equal to its arrival time plus its relative deadline, while each HI-criticality job is assigned a deadline equal to its arrival time plus the smaller of its LO-criticality deadline parameter and x times its HI-criticality deadline parameter. b) At each instant the earliest-deadline waiting job is selected for execution (ties broken arbitrarily).

c) If a job of some task τ i does not complete upon receiving up to C i (LO) units of execution, or arrives earlier than T i (LO) time units after the arrival of the previous job of the same task, then Γ ← HI. 3) Once (Γ ≡ HI) -this corresponds to the third phase of our algorithm, which may or may not happen during any given run of the system a) All currently-active LO-criticality jobs are immediately discarded. The deadline of each currently active HI- criticality job is changed to become equal to its arrival time plus the HI-criticality relative deadline (the D i (HI)) of the task that generated it). That is, if a job of τ i that was released at some time t is active, its deadline, for scheduling purposes, is henceforth t + D i (HI). b) If a job of τ i arrives at some time t, it is assigned a deadline equal to t + D i (HI) if χ i = HI, and discarded if χ i = LO. c) At each instant the earliest-deadline waiting job is selected for execution (ties broken arbitrarily). 4) An additional rule could specify the circumstances when Γ gets reset to LO. This could happen, for instance, if no HI-criticality jobs are active at some instant in time. (We will not discuss the process of resetting Γ ← LO any further in this document.)

div.head: IV. ALGORITHM EDFVD + : PROOF OF CORRECTNESS
div.p: In this section, we will show that if Algorithm EDFVD + declares success for a given task system τ , then τ is scheduled correctly by the run-time dispatcher of Section III-B. Observe that Algorithm EDFVD + may declare success at two places: at lines 4 and 7; we consider each case separately, in Sections IV-A and IV-B.

div.head: A. Algorithm EDFVD + returns success at Line 4
div.p: Suppose that the condition of Line 2 evaluates to true for some task system τ . Recall that LO denotes the load of all the tasks in τ in any LO-criticality behavior (Expression 2), while HI denotes the load of only the HI-criticality tasks in τ in any HI-criticality behavior (Expression 3). For any sequence of job arrivals for τ , consider a (hypothetical) fluid schedule constructed according to the following rules.

• Partition the computing capacity of the unit-speed processor into two virtual processors denoted P L and P H , of computing speeds equal to LO and HI respectively. • Whenever a job of a LO-criticality task τ i arrives at time t o , it is assigned a budget C i (LO) and a deadline at (t o + D i (LO)) upon the virtual processor P L . • Whenever a job of a HI-criticality task τ i arrives at time t o it is assigned both 1) a budget C i (LO) and a deadline at (t o + D i (LO)) on the virtual processor P L , and 2) a budget C i (HI) and a deadline at (t o + D i (HI)) on the virtual processor P H .
• Each virtual processor is scheduled separately using EDF.
• If HI-criticality behavior is detected (Γ ← HI) at some instant during run-time then no LO-criticality jobs are subsequently admitted.

The workload on the virtual processor P L is thus generated only by LO-criticality jobs of all tasks, while the workload on the virtual processor P H is generated by HI-criticality jobs of only the HI-criticality tasks. Since the capacity of P L is equal to LO and the capacity of P H , HI , this hypothetical schedule will therefore meet all deadlines for all jobs of all tasks in all LO-criticality behaviors, and for all jobs of all HIcriticality tasks in all HI-criticality behaviors. In other words, this schedule is correct for scheduling τ , with correctness defined as in Section II.

It is evident that with x ← 1, Algorithm EDFVD + is essentially emulating the EDF scheduling algorithm on the collection of jobs admitted into this virtual schedule. It follows from the optimality (and sustainability [6], [10]) of EDF for scheduling regular (i.e., not mixed-criticality) workloads that Algorithm EDFVD + will therefore also meet all deadlines for all jobs of all tasks in all LO-criticality behaviors, and for all jobs of all HI-criticality tasks in all HI-criticality behaviors. We have thus shown that Lemma 1: If Algorithm EDFVD + returns success at Line 4 for a given task system τ , then τ is scheduled correctly by the run-time dispatcher described in Section III-B.

We now turn our attention to HI-criticality behaviors -in analyzing such behaviors below, we will make extensive use of some techniques and ideas that were introduced in [5] for analyzing dual-criticality systems in which two values are specified only for WCETs, and subsequently applied in [2] to systems in which two values are specified only for the period parameters.

Let us derive conditions that are necessary in order for a deadline miss to occur in some HI-criticality behavior of τ . Let I denote a minimal collection of jobs generated by τ for which a deadline miss occurs, and let t f denote the earliest instant at which a deadline is missed in the schedule for Isee Figure 4. By Lemma 2, we know that this could not have happened in any LO-criticality behavior; hence the run-time algorithm must have set the criticality level indicator Γ to HI prior to time instant t f , and the job to miss its deadline at t f must be of a HI-criticality task. Let t * denote the time instant at which Γ ← HI.

Fact 2: Any job that receives execution during the time interval [t * , t f ) must have its deadline be ≤ t f . Proof: Fact 2 is easily proved by contradiction. Suppose there is a job that has deadline larger than t f , that is executed between t * and t f , and let [t 1 , t 2 ) denote an interval during which this job executes. This implies that during [t 1 , t 2 ) there are no active jobs awaiting execution that have deadline at most t f . Hence the collection of jobs obtained by considering only jobs with arrival time at least t 2 will also miss a deadline at t f ; this contradicts the assumed minimality of I.

Let S * ⊆ I denote the set of jobs that receive execution after t * (see Figure 4). Let J o be the job in S * that has the earliest arrival time. Let a o denote its arrival time, and d o its absolute deadline (i.e., if J o is a job of τ i that was released at time instant a o , then
div.formula: d o = a o + D H i ). Let do denote its scaled deadline: do = a o + min(D L i , x D H i ). (Observe that this implies that do ≤ a o + x D H i .) Fact 3: Any LO-criticality job in I must have its deadline be ≤ a 0 + x(t f -a 0 ).

div.formula: do ≤ a o + x(d o -a o ) ≤ a o + x(t f -a o ), applying the result of Fact 2 to conclude that d o ≤ t f .
div.p: We first will show that no LO-criticality job that has a deadline larger than do will execute at or after a o . This is shown by contradiction:
• Any such job will only receive execution after J o completes (since its deadline is assumed to be larger than do ).
• Any such job will only receive execution prior to time instant t * (since no LO-criticality job executes after t * ).
Taken together, these facts imply that J 0 has completed execution by time instant t * , thereby contradicting the definition of J 0 .

To complete the proof, we next show that any LO-criticality job that executes prior to a o must have its deadline be ≤ do . This, too, is shown by contradiction. Suppose there is a LO- criticality job with absolute deadline > do that executes prior to time instant a o ; consider the latest time instant during which it executes. It must be the case that there are no active jobs with deadline at most do awaiting execution at this time instant, and the job sequence obtained by only considering jobs released after this time instant also misses a deadline. That contradicts the assumed minimality of I.

ALGORITHM EDFVD + : PROPERTIES In Section IV above, we proved that Algorithm EDFVD + of Section III-A, when used in conjunction with the run-time dispatcher of Section III-B, represents a correct scheduling strategy for dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task systems in which two estimates are provided for each of the three parameters that characterize a task. In this section, we provide an evaluation of our scheduling algorithm.
In Figure 5 we depict the feasibility region of Algorithm EDFVD + as a function of the parameters LO and HI characterizing a dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task system τ .

The curve HI = 4(1 -LO )/(4 -LO ) is depicted in Figure 5; any task system for which LO and HI falls below this curve is successfully scheduled by Algorithm EDFVD + in conjunction with the run-time dispatcher of Section III-B. Summarizing the above discussion, we conclude that (i) task systems with parameters falling outside the outer square cannot be guaranteed to be correctly scheduled by any algorithm; (ii) task systems with parameters falling between the curved line and the axes are guaranteed to be scheduled correctly using Algorithm EDFVD + ; and (iii) we do not know whether task systems falling between the outer square and the curved line are schedulable by some other algorithm or not.

Speedup factor. The speedup factor metric is widely used in real-time scheduling as a metric quantifying the effectiveness of non-optimal scheduling algorithms. The speedup factor of a scheduling algorithm A is defined to be the smallest positive real number b ≥ 1, such that any task system schedulable by an optimal clairvoyant scheduler upon a unit-speed processor is also schedulable by algorithm A upon a speed-b processor.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: We have considered the very general model for mixedcriticality 3-parameter sporadic systems proposed by Burns and Davis [12], in which multiple estimates, at varying levels of assurance, may be provided for each of the three parameters WCET, relative deadline, and period that characterize each task. We have generalized the widely-studied EDF-VD mixedcriticality scheduling algorithm [4] to be applicable to the scheduling of task systems represented using this more general model It is known [5,Theorem 4.10] that EDF-VD exhibits a speedup bound of (1 + √ 3/2) in scheduling dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task systems in which two values are specified only for WCETs. The same bound was recently shown [2] to also hold for systems in which two values are specified only for the period parameters of tasks; we have proved here that our generalization to EDF-VD retains this speedup bound when scheduling dual-criticality 3-parameter sporadic task systems with two values specified for each of WCETs, relative deadlines, and periods.

We would like to stress that our attempt in this paper has been to obtain an algorithm with the best speedup bound that we could; we have not listed further pragmatic improvements that seem to often provide better performance (but without improving the speedup factor).

It would be interesting and important to extend our techniques and results to systems with more than two criticality levels specified. Although we know how to generalize the algorithm to this manner, we have not been able to obtain closed-form speedup bounds for the generalized algorithmindeed, obtaining such closed-form speedup bounds remains open even for the simpler, and far more widely studied, problem in which multiple specifications are provided only along the WCET problem. We leave this as future work.
